title: Using Geographic Variation in College Proximity to Estimate the Return to Schooling
research_question: What is the causal effect of an additional year of schooling on individual earnings? The paper seeks to determine whether the wage premium associated with education reflects the productive return to schooling or instead reflects unobserved ability and family background that jointly determine schooling and earnings.
data_description: The analysis uses microdata on young men from the National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men (NLSYM), which began in 1966 with respondents aged 14-24 and followed them through subsequent waves. Key variables include hourly or weekly wages, completed years of schooling, age, labor market experience, race, region of residence, and indicators of family background such as parental education. The analysis also incorporates a geographic variable indicating whether the respondent grew up in a local labor market that contained a four-year college, constructed by matching county of residence in 1966 to the location of accredited colleges. The unit of observation is the individual worker, with earnings measured in the 1976 follow-up wave.
institutional_context: The setting is the U.S. labor market for men entering adulthood in the 1960s and 1970s, a period when access to higher education varied substantially across local areas. Many young men attended college near their family home because of the high costs of relocating, so growing up in a county with a nearby four-year college lowered the effective cost of pursuing post-secondary schooling. Geographic differences in college availability across U.S. counties therefore generated variation in educational attainment that was plausibly unrelated to individual ability or tastes for schooling. This spatial disparity in access — between youths raised in college-adjacent areas and otherwise similar youths raised farther from any college — provides the institutional backdrop for comparing schooling outcomes and later earnings across groups exposed to different educational opportunities.
